statmodels7

statmodels7 is the modeling layer of the statmodels7 toolkit, and the package that installs the rest of it. statmod() reads one formula carrying an equation for every parameter of a distribution and fits it, with any term of modelterms7 in any of those equations.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/statmodels7")

Attaching it attaches the eight member packages.

library(statmodels7)
#> -- Attaching the statmodels7 toolkit 0.203.3
#> v basis7         0.15.1   v numericals7    0.23.3
#> v distributions7 0.80.2   v optimizers7    0.15.1
#> v linkfunctions7 0.5.4    v parameters7    0.26.0
#> v modelterms7    0.99.3   v penalties7     0.33.0

Fitting a model

The equations are separated by a bar, one for each parameter of the distribution, and a parameter with no equation of its own is given an intercept. Below, the mean carries a penalized smooth of x and a random intercept over g, and the standard deviation is linear in x on its log scale.

set.seed(1)
n <- 400
d <- data.frame(x = runif(n, min = -2, max = 2),
                g = factor(rep(1:20, length.out = n)))
u <- rnorm(20, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
d$y <- sin(2 * d$x) + u[as.integer(d$g)] + rnorm(n, sd = exp(-0.7 + 0.4 * d$x))

fit <- statmod(y ~ s(x) + random(~ 1 | g) | sigma ~ x,
               distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = d)

The smoothing parameter of the smooth and the scale of the random effect are hyperparameters. They are estimated by REML, whose gradient and Hessian are computed exactly, and hyper() reports each value with its source: the criterion that estimated it, or fixed for a value held in the term.

hyper(fit)
#>   parameter           term   name  estimate  held source   id
#> 1        mu           s(x) lambda 1.3774223 FALSE   reml <NA>
#> 2        mu random(~1 | g)  sigma 0.5804077 FALSE   reml <NA>

summary() prints the coefficients and the hyperparameters of each equation, with the effective degrees of freedom of each penalized term.

summary(fit)
#> A statmod fit
#> 
#> Call:  statmod(formula = y ~ s(x) + random(~1 | g) | sigma ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), 
#>             data = d)
#> 
#> Distribution: gaussian1     Observations: 400
#> 
#> === mu   [identity link]
#> 
#> Parametric terms
#>                estimate     se      z      p   lower  upper
#>   (Intercept)   0.02975 0.1332 0.2234 0.8233 -0.2313 0.2908
#> 
#> s(x)   [9 coefficients, edf 6.81]
#>                  estimate     se    z        p  lower  upper
#>   lambda [reml]     1.377 0.8096               0.4353  4.359
#>   lin              0.2184 0.0354 6.17 6.83e-10 0.1491 0.2878
#> 
#> random(~1 | g)   [20 coefficients, edf 18.45]
#>                 estimate      se  lower  upper
#>   sigma [reml]    0.5804 0.09696 0.4184 0.8052
#>   predicted effects (20 levels of g)
#>                  Min. 1st Qu.   Median Mean 3rd Qu.  Max.
#>     (Intercept)  -1.1 -0.3411 0.008096    0  0.2206 1.151
#> 
#> === sigma   [log link]
#> 
#> Parametric terms
#>                estimate      se      z       p  lower   upper
#>   (Intercept)   -0.6693 0.03661 -18.28 < 1e-16 -0.741 -0.5976
#>   x              0.3736 0.03385  11.04 < 1e-16 0.3072  0.4399
#> 
#> 95% intervals, bayesian variance
#> conditional log-likelihood -282.744059    effective df 28.26
#> cAIC 622.006    cBIC 734.801
#> fitted in 1.99 s
#> inner   max |grad|/se 1.9e-15   min eigen 0.014
#> outer   max |grad|/se 2.9e-12   min eigen 0.97
#> 1 note: print(summary(fit), notes = TRUE)

After the conditional log-likelihood and the information criteria, the table ends with two lines headed inner and outer. Each gives the largest gradient in standard errors and the smallest eigenvalue of the curvature, for the coefficients and for the hyperparameters respectively, and both are read at the point that the fit reached.

statmod_certificate() is computed at the same point and not read off the stopping rule of the optimizer. Its mode_error is how far above its own penalized mode the coefficients stopped, in log-likelihood units, and its state is converged, boundary, not converged or unknown.

statmod_certificate(fit)[c("state", "mode_error")]
#> $state
#> [1] "converged"
#> 
#> $mode_error
#> [1] 4.831658e-30

predict() returns the fitted value of any parameter, or of a moment of the response, with a standard error that follows from every term in the model.

predict(fit, what = "mu", newdata = head(d, n = 3), se = TRUE)
#>           fit        se      lower      upper
#> 1 -0.81384092 0.1046663 -1.0189830 -0.6086988
#> 2  0.06690214 0.1012942 -0.1316309  0.2654351
#> 3  1.41682665 0.1327520  1.1566376  1.6770157

What the layer fits

Any term of modelterms7 goes in any equation: the parametric block, penalized smooths of one and several covariates, grouped random intercepts and slopes, ridge, lasso, elastic net, SCAD and MCP, a nonlinear parametric term, effects that change at estimated break-points, score-driven dynamics and latent Markov regimes. A formula carries at most one score-driven term, regime term or break-point term built with marginal = TRUE. A score-driven term is fitted in one system with the coefficients, and vcov() is built from the observed information of that joint model. A regime term, or a marginal break-point term, is fitted by alternating with the coefficients.

The hyperparameters of a smooth penalty are estimated by reml() or ml(), or by aic() or bic() on an estimate of prediction error, all passed as outer_criterion. A penalty with a kink (lasso(), enet(), scad() and mcp()) has no second derivative at the mode, so its hyperparameter is chosen along a path of its own values, from the value that empties the block downwards. The path is scored by sparse_criterion, which is bic() by default and may also be aic() or cv(). The function cv() serves only as sparse_criterion.

Random effects written with the same label and the same grouping share one covariance block, in whichever equation they appear, as with the middle bar of (1 | u | id) in brms. The formula y ~ random(~ 1 | u | id) | sigma ~ random(~ 1 | u | id) estimates the correlation between a subject’s level and the logarithm of its scale. The label reaches a subformula too, so seg(x, psi ~ random(~ 1 | u | id)) in the same formula correlates a random break-point with a random scale. The block is one multivariate prior over the effects of one level, parametrized by dr_prod() by default, whose free coordinates are the logarithms of the standard deviations followed by the angles of the correlation.

rstatmod() simulates from a model written the same way and returns the parameters used beside the data.

sim <- rstatmod(y ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = d[1:20, ],
                par = list(mu = c(1, 2), sigma = log(0.3)))
sim$par
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>           1           2 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept) 
#>   -1.203973

The vignette fitting a distributional model works through a fit from the formula to the fitted object.

The toolkit in one package

Installing this package installs the eight members, and attaching it attaches them. The members are listed in Imports and attached by the package itself, which prints one message with the version of each; Depends would attach them without a report.

statmodels7_packages()
#> [1] "basis7"         "distributions7" "linkfunctions7" "modelterms7"   
#> [5] "numericals7"    "optimizers7"    "parameters7"    "penalties7"
package what it provides
numericals7 the numerical layer at the root: stencils, batched quadrature and series, the combinatorial enumerations, special functions
linkfunctions7 link functions as objects, with exact derivatives to fifth order in both directions
distributions7 univariate and multivariate distributions with exact score, information and higher derivatives
optimizers7 optimization algorithms as objects, with composable stopping rules
basis7 basis expansions with derivatives, anchored integrals and exact Gram matrices
parameters7 constrained parameters as maps from an unconstrained vector, exact to fourth order
penalties7 penalties as objects, with exact derivatives, proximal operators and the pieces that a marginal criterion consumes
modelterms7 model terms as objects, each carrying its design block, its penalty and its blueprint for new data

statmodels7_versions() reports the installed version of each member, statmodels7_conflicts() the names that members mask from one another, and statmodels7_update(action = "install") installs or updates every member.

Related

The mathematical companion to the toolkit is the book, which presents the formulas that the packages implement, explains where each quantity comes from and cites the source of the full argument.
